title: This one pleases me (Genesis Rabbah 3:7)
hookLine: God built worlds and unmade them, then said of this one: it pleases me
tomorrow: before people were made, who in heaven voted no?

cards: Every group project has a folder of abandoned versions: version one, version two, final, final-final. Here's a line that sounds like it came out of that folder.
In Genesis, before there's any sun, the text says: "And there was evening and there was morning, one day." Look at the wording. Not "let there be evening."
There was evening, as if evenings already had a way of happening. Some rabbis took that small phrase as a clue that this wasn't the first version.

teach.h: THERE WAS EVENING, NOT LET THERE BE.
teach.b: Genesis Rabbah gives two voices. Rabbi Yehudah bar Simon says the wording shows an order of time already existed.

Rabbi Abbahu goes further, and his is the line people repeat: the Holy One kept creating worlds and destroying them, until He created this one. Then He said: this one pleases Me; those did not please Me.
Sit with how strange that is, a day after the blueprint.
The same tradition that says God looked into a perfect plan also tells of worlds built and unbuilt. The midrash never says what was wrong with them. It doesn't describe them at all.
It keeps only the verdict. And look at what the verdict isn't.

It isn't "this one is perfect." This is the world with a flood and jealous brothers still ahead, the world whose own story, a few chapters on, has God regretting making people. Still: this one pleases Me.
So the plan and the versions belong together. A good plan doesn't promise the first try works.
It means you know what you're building well enough to recognize it when it's in front of you, and to stop tearing down. Pleased doesn't mean finished.
It means: this one, I'll keep.

how: Rabbi Abbahu's saying is part of the midrash on the first chapter of Genesis, often read in study groups when the Torah reading cycle starts again in the fall.

games.q: what does “this one pleases me” mean?
o: God's praise for one person who obeyed
God's verdict on this world, after other versions
a blessing said over a meal that tastes good

games.q: who says what about the versions — tap the pairs.
p: an order of time existed before
the odd wording that starts it

s: the midrash says this world is perfect
it says this one pleases Me, a world still headed for a flood and quarrels.
the midrash describes what was wrong with the earlier worlds
it keeps only the verdict, not the versions.
the clue is a small wording in Genesis 1
there was evening, not let there be evening.

games.q: you've rewritten your college essay five times. a friend says it's good. by Rabbi Abbahu's story, what's the move?
o: keep tearing it down until nothing in it could be better.
recognize the one that's yours, say this one, and keep it.
go back to version one; first instincts are always right.
games.why: in the midrash the versions end with a verdict, not perfection: this one pleases Me.

practice: Take a scrap of paper and write one sentence by hand about something you care about, with no planning. Don't cross anything out.
Read it once, leave it exactly as it is, and rest your eyes on it for the sit: a first version you're allowed to keep.

wordCard.voice: This one pleases me: Rabbi Abbahu's line in Genesis Rabbah, after worlds were built and unbuilt. Not perfect. Kept.

orig.note: Hebrew: and there was evening (Genesis 1:5), the wording the midrash reads as a clue.

carryVoice: Keep this one: this one pleases me, and a version can be the one. See you tomorrow.
